title: Before dawn, a hymn to Christ
author: Pliny the Younger

edition.name: Pliny, Selected Letters, Dickinson College Commentaries, "Edited by Ashley Roman Francese" (as credited on the page); the page does not name the critical edition its Latin follows. edition.section: Letter 10.96.7 (first sentence) and Trajan's reply 10.97.2 (first sentence)

source_text: Adfirmabant autem hanc fuisse summam vel culpae suae vel erroris, quod essent soliti stato die ante lucem convenire, carmenque Christo quasi deo dicere secum invicem seque sacramento non in scelus aliquod obstringere, sed ne furta ne latrocinia ne adulteria committerent, ne fidem fallerent, ne depositum adpellati abnegarent. … Conquirendi non sunt; si deferantur et arguantur, puniendi sunt, ita tamen ut, qui negaverit se Christianum esse idque re ipsa manifestum fecerit, id est supplicando dis nostris, quamvis suspectus in praeteritum, veniam ex paenitentia impetret.
excerpt_note: Two passages joined: the first sentence of Pliny's 10.96.7, then (after the ellipsis, which is Vocābula's, not the edition's) the first sentence of Trajan's reply, 10.97.2, from the separate DCC page https://dcc.dickinson.edu/pliny-letters/10-97. The DCC text prints macrons; they are removed here for tracing. The Perseus text of the letters (edition unnamed) spells Affirmabant and appellati.

translation: They declared, however, that the sum of their guilt, or their error, had been this: they used to meet on a fixed day before daybreak and chant a hymn among themselves, taking turns, to Christ as to a god, and to bind themselves by an oath, not to commit some crime, but not to commit theft, banditry or adultery, not to break their word, and, when asked to hand back money left in their care, not to claim they had never received it. … [Trajan:] They are not to be hunted down. If they are reported and proved guilty, they must be punished, but on this condition: anyone who denies he is a Christian and proves it by his actions, that is, by praying to our gods, shall obtain pardon through repentance, even if he was under suspicion before.
translation_note: Pliny's sentence is reported speech after Adfirmābant: infinitives (fuisse, convenīre, dīcere, obstringere) and subjunctives (essent, committerent). Sēcum invicem probably means the chant was sung responsively, but "among themselves in turn" is the literal sense. Trajan's gerundives (conquīrendī, pūniendī) express obligation. Negāverit and fēcerit can be read as future perfect indicatives or perfect subjunctives; English uses the present.

essay.t: Pliny governed Bithynia and Pontus, on the Black Sea coast of Asia Minor, as Trajan's legate with consular power; an inscription (CIL V 5262) records the title.

Normally run by a proconsul, the province was made temporarily imperial, the Judaism and Rome project explains, so Trajan could choose the governor after years of financial trouble and factional disorder.
The dates are uncertain: Livius gives 109–111, the Judaism and Rome project "probably" 110–112. His death is placed about 113 by Britannica and about 115 by Livius; both are estimates.
Elsewhere in Book 10, Pliny asks to form a guild of 150 firemen at Nicomedia after a fire; Trajan refuses: in that province any such group would soon become a political club, a hetaeria.
Here, the Christians said they had stopped their common meal after Pliny's edict, issued on Trajan's instructions, banned hetaeriae.
My reading: facing a new problem, the governor applied an existing rule and asked the centre, which declined to make a general law.
Pliny admits he had never attended a trial of Christians and did not know whether the name itself was punishable or only attached crimes.
He questioned the accused three times, executed those who persisted, sent citizens to Rome, and released those who invoked the gods, offered incense and wine to Trajan's image and cursed Christ.
Trajan approved: Christians were not to be sought out, but if accused and convicted were punished unless they recanted by praying to the gods; anonymous accusations were barred.
The legal basis is debated: Sherwin-White held that obstinacy (contumacia) was punished; others posit an existing law.
Classic papers: de Ste. Croix (1963) and Sherwin-White's reply; I checked only their bibliographic records.
Tertullian later summed up the ruling: not to be sought out, but punished if brought forward.
This is rare outside testimony to early Christian worship, but it comes from people under interrogation, some former members, and may reflect what they hoped would save them.
Torturing two slave women called ministrae, "deaconesses", Pliny found nothing but "a depraved and excessive superstition".

questions.q: What did Trajan rule about Christians?
options: Not to be hunted down, but punished if convicted
To be hunted down in every city of the province
To be released whether convicted or not
To be sent to Rome for trial by the emperor

questions.q: Which other exchange shows the same worry about associations?
options: Trajan refused a firemen's guild at Nicomedia
Trajan refused a new aqueduct at Nicomedia
Trajan banned athletic games in Bithynia
Trajan closed the temples of Nicomedia

questions.q: How could the accused show they were not Christians?
options: By praying to the gods and cursing Christ
By paying a fine to the governor
By swearing an oath on their own lives
By leaving the province for good
